paragraphs.source_en: At the Tin Tazarift composition, the men with bows might represent elder hunters already initiated, and the others without bows young men on their passage to the manhood. This may be supported by another fact: the only animal here, an antelope, may represent the first game killed (considering its great importance also in the Round Head art) and it is superimposed onto the "flying" man's hand. The antelope conveys further important information. In the Round Head art, both animals and male anthropomorphic figures almost never have their sexual organs represented, but this antelope's penis is carefully depicted in order to indicate the maleness. Why was this specification important? Is there any connection between the male antelope and the decorated man?

paragraphs.source_en: This interpretation, although inspired by the ethnographic record, is subjective. It nevertheless shows that more ways have to be investigated in the search of the meaning. Hallier & Hallier (2010) proposed that the "flying" figures could be in fact swimming, but they do not explain why prehistoric people would enter into the water adorned with body painting, horns, bracelets and other adornments. Another interpretation of this scene was proposed by Soleilhavoup (2005; 2007), as a shamans' out-of-body travel in an altered state of consciousness. I do not exclude a possible representation of people in trance but the "flying" figures may represent another imaginary travel–that of the passage from one social stage into another; a process of making new hunters. According to this hypothesis, this shelter may have been used for young men's initiation and/or rituals.

paragraphs.source_en: Another frequent element in the ethnographic record is the importance of masks and their abundant use in rituals and ceremonies, mainly in African culture (Willett 1971). The masks are not simple objects of art but they possess their own spirit and they are therefore very powerful, especially during the rituals for which they were made. African masks are of numerous kinds and functions, for example in the Dogon culture the most important category is that of animals, represented by fifteen different masks (Palau Marti 1957). Masks are used in various occasions, the most frequent being those related to the death and ancestors, and to (especially male) initiations. After the ritual, masks have to be deposited in secret places until the next use (Gillon 1984).
